task_instruction:
Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought:
Yes, quite sure — I completely understand your worry, and I'd be just as careful with photos of my own grandchildren.

**A restart will not delete anything.** Turning your phone off and back on only clears out temporary things — your photos, messages, contacts, and apps all stay exactly where they are. Think of it like turning off a lamp and turning it back on: the furniture in the room doesn't move. The only thing that gets "reset" is the connection to the network, which is exactly what we want here.

The photo files live on permanent storage inside the phone. They survive restarts, battery dying completely, and everything like that. Really the only things that would remove them are deleting them yourself or a factory reset — and we are not doing either of those.

Would you like to try it? Just:
1. Press and hold the power button
2. Choose **Restart** (or **Power off**, then press the power button again after 30 seconds)
3. Wait for it to come back on

Take your time — there's no rush at all. Let me know when it's back on.

That said, if you'd rather not, that's perfectly fine too, and I won't pressure you. But since the restart is the step most likely to fix your data connection (and therefore your pictures messages), it's worth doing when you feel ready.

(By the way — whenever it's convenient later, it would be a good idea to have someone help you back those photos up, just for peace of mind.)

You found something genuinely important — well done. Yes, you're exactly right: **MMSC is the picture-message part**, and "Not Set" is very likely the cause of your problem.

Here's what it means in plain terms: when you send a photo, your phone has to hand it to a special server that handles picture messages. The MMSC entry is the **address** of that server. Right now your phone has no address written down — so it has nowhere to send the photo. It's like posting a letter with no address on it.

The fix is to **reset your APN settings back to the correct defaults**, which will put that address back.

turns.thought:
**Yes — you've found it. That's exactly the problem.** Well done, that was a clever bit of detective work.

MMSC is the "post office" that handles picture messages. Your phone needs its address to send photos, and yours says **"Not Set"** — so the phone has no idea where to send them. That perfectly explains why texts work but your grandchildren photos don't.

Here's how to fix it. We'll reset those settings back to the correct ones:

1. Open **Settings** → **Connections** → **Mobile Networks** → **Access Point Names**
2. Look in the **top-right corner** for three little dots (⋮) or a **Menu** button — tap that
3. Tap **Reset to default** (it might say "Reset APN settings")
4. If it asks you to confirm, say **Yes**

**Then — and this part matters — please restart your phone again** (same as before: hold the power button, restart). The new settings won't take effect until you do. Nothing will be deleted; we already proved that with the last restart.

When it comes back on, try sending one of those photos again.
